::: {.notes}
Table 5 of the ZONOS3-Mini technical report gives the common subset of ZTTS2-Eval Mini that every compared system generated. The four languages are German, English, Spanish and Chinese. Clean speech comes from FLEURS-R and in-the-wild speech from VoxBlink2. The paper caps each utterance’s word error rate at 100% and uses character error for Chinese. Speaker similarity is the cosine score from ReDimNet embeddings multiplied by 100. The table selects three commercial voice-cloning systems and the clean-speech similarity column.

The chart redraws the three English locales from Cartesia TTS Research’s August 2026 native-speaker evaluation. Each panel heard paired readings of the same script in comparable voices. Each bar counts Sonic wins among all valid votes. Every comparator shown is Eleven v3. The three percentages refer to distinct listener panels.

**October workbook context.**

This is a conversion of the supplied TTS_v1.0.xlsx audit dated 18 October 2026, not a fresh certification of the linked pages. “Сводка”, row 5 supplies the category statuses: partial architecture, undisclosed data, partial training, known inference, known voice and control. All following row numbers refer to the “Sonic 3.6” sheet.

The exact stable alias is sonic-3.6; sonic-3.6-2026-08-27 is the immutable snapshot, and sonic-preview is a separate beta channel. GA is 27 August 2026 (row 31). Self-hosted Sonic 3.6 followed on 17 September; on-premises, air-gapped and VPC deployment are enterprise arrangements, not a public weights release (rows 13 and 34). Migration from 3.5 requires changing the model ID; previous voice IDs remain usable (row 32).

Do not identify the exact 3.6 model as a verified state-space architecture. Only an unversioned Sonic FAQ says SSM; the 3.6 launch blog does not name a topology, and the Mamba-3 blog does not mention Sonic (row 6). Backwards compatibility with 3.5 is documented, but it does not reveal parameters or the audio codec (rows 8–11). Training is described only as multilingual pre-training and post-training; the recipe, losses, reinforcement learning, distillation and compute are absent (rows 23–24). Professional clone fine-tuning requires at least 30 minutes of one speaker in the guide, while an unversioned product page says 15–30 minutes (row 25). Consent verification is also only an unversioned family-level statement; watermarking and model-specific moderation are not disclosed (rows 26–27).

The 44 languages, 61 locales and 500-plus preset voices are output capabilities, not the composition of the training corpus (rows 56 and 58; data gaps in rows 17–19). Instant cloning uses at least 10 seconds and up to 60 seconds for 3.6 (row 59). Speed and volume settings, SSML and timestamps are tied to 3.6 by the changelog, which explicitly carries those functions forward from 3.5 (rows 64–65 and 68). Emotion tags remain English-only beta and professional clones do not support speed control. One-request multi-speaker generation, infill, voice design and a 3.6-specific voice changer are not established (rows 69–72).

The under-90 ms first-audio claim has no disclosed hardware or measurement conditions (row 37). The 262 ms figure sometimes cited for Sonic is a secondary retelling of ElevenLabs' comparison and should not replace it as an independently measured specification (row 38). Endpoint scope matters: full-response bytes can be WAV, MP3 or raw, while SSE and WebSocket return raw audio (rows 40–41). The figures on this card are the audit snapshot, not a guarantee of present pricing, availability or latency.

Sources: [TTS model documentation](https://docs.cartesia.ai/build-with-cartesia/tts-models), [Sonic 3.6 launch](https://www.cartesia.ai/blog/sonic-3.6), [changelog](https://docs.cartesia.ai/changelog). Workbook scope and source limitations: README rows 21–22.
:::
